cards.title: GitHub's new Git storage architecture

depth.text: GitHub built new storage so **thousands of agents** can push to **one repository** at once

In internal tests, it handled **5,000 concurrent agents** and **7,200 pushes per second** on one repository. Git objects live in Azure Blob Storage, while references go in **Ref-CAS**, a separate replicated log service; virtual replicas serve requests while dedicated compaction nodes merge packs.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see this as preparation for agent-driven repository traffic; others question whether thousands of pushes per second are a good idea or whether the design addresses current outages.

cards.title: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2

depth.text: someone broke out of a **Firecracker virtual machine** and made its host run code as **root**

They traced a **guest memory page** back to the host process, then changed the live vCPU thread’s **saved registers** so Firecracker called its write wrapper when it returned from KVM. A **serial-port write** triggered the call; this test had no jailer, while production containment can drop privileges and restrict Firecracker through namespaces and seccomp.

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter says the write-up is informative; another calls it “pure LLM slop.”

comments.text: I really wish they would have expanded on this paragraph in their article further: > The configuration used here had no jailer. Firecracker's production containment includes dropping privileges and restricting the process through namespaces and seccomp. A deployment using those controls requires a separate assessment of the privileges and resources available after compromising its VMM. If I'm…

I am more convinced by the day that the Nova Microhypervisor approach is correct. Do virtualization with a tiny formally verified microkernel and have complex kernels like Linux run underneath instead of letting a huge, complex, and brittle linux kernel and vm ecosystem control the hypervisor layer. https://hypervisor.org/

I have a demo service that entirely relies on Firecracker VMs: ClickBench playground, https://benchmark.clickhouse.com/playground/ It hosts hundreds of database engines - many of them have vulnerabilities, and some of them, like Pandas, are basically open RCEs regardless. We can PoC the Firecracker VM Escape on that service.

This is not a new vulnerability, it's just a description of how to exploit the PwnEscape vulnerability in practice on firecracker VMs (disclosed multiple weeks ago and discussed in some less upvoted posts on HN)

Pretty interesting approach, compared to receiving a zillion potentially sloppy PRs. Open source in the age of LLMs.. ("agent source"?)
> Every app can run headless, so an agent can render to PNG, dump the element tree and drive it with scripted input. This is cool. I hope SwiftUI / UIKit borrow this idea for native mac apps.

Does this have: - Accessibility? E.g. Screen reader support? - Alternative inputs? Full keyboard support? - Full internationalization, including right-to-left and diacritics? What happens when no GPU is available? Just curious as this matters for it to be a serious library and not a proof of concept.

How should I think about this, compared to GPUI ( https://gpui.rs )?
What are pros and cons?

cards.title: We've built an open-source feature flag server for 11 years

depth.text: someone built an **open-source** tool for **switching features** on and off without redeploying

Unleash creator Ivar says it began as an **internal tool** in **2014**. Its server-side SDKs fetch flag config, then evaluate it inside your app, so user data stays there and a flag check is a **memory lookup**, not a network call.

cards.camps: Two camps: skeptics say a server for booleans adds infrastructure; supporters say the service has real value for teams that want it.

comments.text: Had a look at their website [1]. Initial thoughts: this is a bit ridiculous, I can just build that myself. And in fact, I have done already. Thoughts after about 3 minutes of browsing: OK, this actually makes sense and I see why people would pay for this. The value proposition is definitely there [1] https://www.getunleash.io/
Yesterday I saw that LaunchDarkly is a $3B company. How crazy is that?!

Are most feature flag systems really just simple Boolean checks like this with no feedback loop? In 2009 Amazon’s equivalent supported multi-variate flags (run test with more than 2 options), a feedback loop for performance/attribution, and
weighting. I don’t see any of that on the unleash home page, but also haven’t seen it in other feature config systems either.

This domain needs some better ontology and taxonomy, there's so many overlapping and conflated terms whenever I hear about it. To name a few: - Feature Flags used as Configs; - Configs used as Feature Flags; - Live Ops, Control Groups, Experiments, Analytics, and more bundled as "extras" to Feature Flags as if they were the right parent term; I think classical systems/engineering see feature…

Cool! Feature flags are great when you need them. I’ve seen so many different implementations of flags over the years. Even made one myself couple years ago which uses a GitHub issue (and a list of checkboxes) as a persistent store for maintaining and toggling with flags. https://github.com/TimMikeladze/next-flag

cards.title: A wave of plastic-free coffee pods and machines

depth.text: coffee brands are launching **less-plastic pods** and machines as shoppers worry about **microplastics**

Lavazza's **Tablì** is a $129 machine for compressed coffee tablets; Keurig's **Alta** has compostable pods that don't fit older machines. Its bundle costs $499. Caraway's $495 machine is stainless steel and glass, so plastic doesn't touch the coffee grounds.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say old-school brewers already avoid plastic cheaply; others like the idea but question whether the new pods taste good enough.

comments.text: Huh, cool. If you want to save a few bucks you can go with a stainless steel French press or a mason jar if you're into cold brews. You're symbolizing a different kind of status though. This summer was sunny and hot in Colorado, so every morning I'd make a jar of sun coffee. I'd leave it out through the day and overnight. The next morning I'd pull it in, filter it, refill it with grounds and…

Hate to be the bearer of bad news, but even the $10k slayer espresso machine has a plastic water resevoir. Granted the brewing assembly is mostly plastic free. While I sympathize with the sentiment to eliminate plastic from the transport chain for anything ingestible, it's practically impossible in the modern world. Simple is usually best; glass or ceramic pour over, stainless press, or even the…
I like Moka pots. Zero plastic But seriously it's a shame how hard it is to find products like coffee makers and electric kettles with no plastic. Heat and plastic don't mix
Aeropress makes a glass version although I was never too concerned about the microplastic risk

I have a Technivorm Moccamaster KBG-V and they use good plastic for their parts but it's still plastic (except the thermal carafe etc). There's a new copycat version that's all glass and plastic (Simply Good I think?) but not sure how it actually performs. What I'm surprised at is that no one has made non-plastic drop-in replacement parts for the reservoir, basket, and funnel. The KBG-V is highly…

glossary.EXPERT flag: A switch in the installer that early M3 users had to turn on before support became generally available.
glossary.Thunderbolt: A connection standard for linking computers with peripherals and each other using a cable.
glossary.XDomain: A feature that lets two Thunderbolt computers connect directly to each other.
glossary.upstream-first: Doing changes in the main shared project first, rather than maintaining them separately and sending them in later.
glossary.GNU General Public License (GPL): GNU General Public License: a software licence that requires people who share changed versions to keep the same licence terms.
glossary.copyleft: A way of licensing code that lets people reuse it but requires shared changed copies to keep the same sharing rules.
glossary.knowledge graph: A way to organize information by showing how people, places, or things are connected.
glossary.daemon: A program that runs in the background and handles a task without being started each time.
glossary.kinship inference: A guess about which people are related, such as who might be family.
glossary.SQLite: A small database that can be stored in a single file.
glossary.TCC Full Disk Access: A macOS permission that gives an app access to files normally kept off limits.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.GDPR: General Data Protection Regulation: a European law that sets rules for how organizations use people's personal information.
glossary.RAM: Random-Access Memory: a computer's working space for information it is using right now.
glossary.mainframe: A large central computer that many people can use, rather than each person having their own computer.
glossary.OOM: Out of memory: when a program runs out of the memory it has available.
glossary.DRAM fab: DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory) fab: a factory that makes chips used as computer memory.
glossary.Ref-CAS: Reference Compare-and-Swap: a service that checks a branch still points where expected before recording a change.
glossary.virtual replica: A replaceable worker that handles repository requests and keeps a local cache that can be rebuilt.
glossary.compaction: Shortening an AI’s conversation history, often by turning it into a summary.
glossary.quorum: The group of checks that must get the right response for validation to pass.
glossary.pack: A bundle of Git data stored together; this system adds packs on pushes and later merges them.
glossary.vertical scale: Handling more developers or agents working in the same repository.
glossary.VM: Virtual machine: a computer that runs inside another computer.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.toolchain: A set of tools used together to get a job done.
glossary.allowlist: A list of apps or people that are allowed to connect.
glossary.proxy: A go-between that gets information from another website on someone else's behalf.
glossary.XSS: Cross-site scripting: A flaw that can make a website run instructions supplied by someone visiting it.
glossary.CDN: Content Delivery Network: A network of servers that helps websites handle requests closer to their users.
glossary.responsible disclosure: Privately reporting a security flaw so its maintainers have time to fix it before it is made public.
glossary.blocklist: A list of files or sources a tool should reject or remove.
glossary.WHOIS: A public lookup service for details about who registered a website name; those details can be hidden or outdated.
glossary.ABI: Application Binary Interface: the agreed rules software uses to communicate with other software.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.opaque handle: A reference you can use to work with something without seeing how it is built inside.
glossary.TUI: Terminal User Interface: the menus and controls an app shows inside a text terminal.
glossary.identity resolution: Matching records from different sources so they point to the right real person.
glossary.over-merging: Combining records from different people as if they belonged to one person.
glossary.confidence calibration: How well a model’s confidence scores match how often it is actually right.
glossary.decision model: A program that weighs possible choices and predicts or selects one.
glossary.hybrid model: A setup that uses one model first and sends selected cases to another for review.
glossary.MS-DOS: Microsoft Disk Operating System: older computer software that runs programs using typed commands.
